quiz.question: Your team uses a Scrum board. Where should a new feature request from sales go first?
options: The product backlog for refinement and prioritization
Directly into the current sprint so sales is unblocked
A new epic flagged as the team's highest priority
Straight to the engineer who owns that product area
quiz.explanation: New requests go into the product backlog, where they are refined and prioritized against everything else. Pulling a request straight into the current sprint skips prioritization and disrupts the commitment the team has already made.

quiz.question: In Jira, the correct hierarchy is:
options: Story > Epic > Task
Sprint > Epic > Story
Board > Task > Epic
Epic > Story > Sub-task
quiz.explanation: Epics contain stories; stories can contain sub-tasks. Sprints and boards are containers for work, not hierarchy levels.

quiz.question: In a product analytics tool, an 'event' is:
options: An attribute attached to a user, such as plan or country
A group of users who signed up in the same week
A recorded user action, such as 'clicked checkout'
A saved chart that tracks a metric over time
quiz.explanation: An event is a tracked user action. Attributes such as plan, device or country are properties, which add context to events or users. A same-week signup group is a cohort, and a saved chart is a report.

quiz.question: Your signup -> activation funnel shows an 80% drop at step 2. What is your first move?
options: Redesign the full onboarding flow to remove step 2
Add a tooltip guide to step 2 and watch the change
A/B test new copy on the step 2 screen right away
Segment the drop-off by device, source, and user type
quiz.explanation: Segment before you solve: the drop may come from one platform, channel or cohort rather than from every user. Jumping to a redesign or a copy test means solving a problem you have not located yet.

quiz.question: A retention chart shows Day-1 60%, Day-7 20%, Day-30 18%. What does the flattening at around 18% suggest?
options: Retention will keep falling toward zero at the same rate
Most users churn, so this shows no sign of product-market fit
A core group found lasting value and forms a retained base
Day-30 data is noisy, so only the Day-7 figure is reliable
quiz.explanation: When a retention curve flattens, a stable group keeps getting value, which is a positive signal. The goal then becomes raising the level where it flattens. Reading the early churn as 'no product-market fit' ignores that the curve stopped falling.

quiz.question: Which SQL query returns the number of signups per day?
options: SELECT date, COUNT(*) FROM signups GROUP BY date
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM signups
SELECT DISTINCT date FROM signups
SELECT date, COUNT(*) FROM signups ORDER BY date
quiz.explanation: COUNT(*) with GROUP BY date gives one row per day with that day's count. Without GROUP BY, COUNT(*) collapses everything into a single total, and ORDER BY only sorts rows without grouping them. Most databases also reject mixing date with COUNT(*) unless you group by date.

quiz.question: Mid-sprint, an executive asks you to add one small story. As Product Owner, you should:
options: Add it, since it is small and leadership has asked for it
Assess it with the team; if urgent, swap out equal scope
Refuse, since sprint scope can never change once started
Cancel the sprint and replan around the new request
quiz.explanation: Sprint scope is protected, but genuine urgency can justify a deliberate, visible trade that the team agrees to and that keeps the sprint goal intact. Flatly refusing is too rigid: Scrum lets the Product Owner and developers renegotiate scope when needed.

quiz.question: Funnels answer 'where do users drop off?' Retention curves answer:
options: What share of users complete each step of a flow
Which acquisition channel brings the most signups
How many unique users are active on a given day
Whether users keep coming back for value over time
quiz.explanation: Retention measures whether users return and keep getting value over time, a key signal of product-market fit. Step-by-step completion is what a funnel measures, and a single day's active-user count tells you nothing about whether users return.

quiz.question: The PM's main job in Jira is:
options: Keeping a prioritized, refined backlog that reflects strategy
Breaking stories into technical sub-tasks for engineers
Tracking velocity and pushing the team to close more tickets
Assigning each ticket to a specific engineer every sprint
quiz.explanation: A prioritized, refined backlog is strategy made executable, and that is the PM's core responsibility in Jira. Engineers usually own the technical breakdown into sub-tasks and decide among themselves who picks up which work.

quiz.question: You want to know whether the new onboarding improved activation. Which comparison is most reliable?
options: Activation of users who opted into the new flow vs those who did not
Activation of randomly assigned new-flow vs old-flow users in the same period
Activation of post-launch signups vs signups from the month before launch
Day-30 retention of all users this month vs the same month last year
quiz.explanation: Randomly assigning users to the new or old flow over the same period isolates the onboarding change, as an A/B test does. Comparing users who opted in adds self-selection bias, because motivated users choose the new flow. A before/after comparison mixes in seasonality, campaigns and shifts in traffic mix.

quiz.question: Which is the best one-line explanation of an API?
options: A shared database that stores data so many applications can query it directly
A defined set of requests one system exposes so other software can use it
A programming language used to connect an app's front end to its back end
A settings screen that lets developers configure how an application behaves
quiz.explanation: An API is a contract: send a request in the defined format and get back a defined response. It is not the database itself. An API often sits in front of a database precisely so other software never queries the database directly.

quiz.question: In a REST API, what does a GET request typically do?
options: Sends new data to the server to create a record, like a user
Reads or fetches data from the server without changing it
Replaces an existing record on the server with values you send
Removes a specified record from the server's database
quiz.explanation: GET reads data, POST creates, PUT/PATCH update, and DELETE removes. Creating a record (the most common mix-up) is POST's job, not GET's.

quiz.question: Your app's error logs show a spike in both 404 and 500 responses from your API. What do these codes indicate?
options: 404: the server is down for maintenance; 500: the request was malformed
404: the user isn't logged in; 500: the client exceeded the rate limit
404: the requested resource wasn't found; 500: the server itself errored
404: the request timed out; 500: the response payload was too large
quiz.explanation: 4xx codes mean something is wrong with the request (404 = not found), and 5xx codes mean the server failed (500 = internal error). The swapped option gets the client/server split backwards, which would send your bug triage to the wrong team.

quiz.question: An engineer says 'that needs a schema migration.' What do they mean?
options: The database structure must change, which adds risk and needs careful testing
The API's request and response format must change for all existing clients
All the data must be moved to a new server or cloud provider before launch
The front-end screens must be rebuilt to match the updated design system
quiz.explanation: A schema migration changes the structure of the database, such as tables, columns or types, underneath live data. It is doable but needs extra testing time. It is not a move to a new host, which is the common misreading of the word 'migration'.

quiz.question: Your feature depends on a third-party API with a 99.9% uptime SLA. What is the best PM approach?
options: Design the failure state: what users see and can still do when it's down
Treat 99.9% as effectively always-on and skip failure handling to ship faster
Build an in-house replacement first so the feature has no external dependency
Rely on the SLA's service credits to cover any losses when the API goes down
quiz.explanation: 0.1% downtime is still about 43 minutes a month, so every external dependency needs a designed fallback, such as cached data or a clear message. SLA credits refund part of your fees, but they do nothing for users who hit a broken screen during the outage.

quiz.question: Your weather widget starts receiving HTTP 429 'Too Many Requests' errors at peak hours. Why do APIs enforce rate limits like this?
options: To block unauthenticated users from reading the API's private data
To keep response payloads small enough for slow mobile networks
To guarantee every request is answered within a fixed response time
To protect the provider's servers from overload and abuse by any one client
quiz.explanation: Rate limits cap how many requests one client can make in a time window, which protects the service from overload and abuse. Your design must respect them, for example through caching or batching. Blocking unauthenticated access is a different job, handled by authentication.

quiz.question: What is JSON?
options: A database engine that stores API responses for later reuse
A JavaScript framework for building the front end of web apps
A human-readable text format APIs commonly use to send data
An encryption method that secures data sent between systems
quiz.explanation: JSON is a key:value text format that most APIs use to exchange data. The weather API response you opened in the exercise was JSON. It describes data but does not store it the way a database does.

quiz.question: A PM wants to know if feature X is feasible. Which question to engineering will usually lead to the most useful conversation?
options: Exactly how many days will it take, so I can commit to a launch date?
What are the main technical approaches, and what are their trade-offs?
Is this technically possible with our current stack, yes or no?
Which engineer is free this sprint to start building it right away?
quiz.explanation: Asking about approaches and trade-offs brings out options, risks and effort ranges that you can scope against. Demanding an exact day count up front tends to produce padded estimates. A yes/no feasibility question hides the cost of each path.

quiz.question: Your weather widget calls a paid API every time any user opens the app, and costs are rising. An engineer suggests caching the response. What does that mean?
options: Deleting outdated responses so the app always shows the newest data
Encrypting the response payload so it can be stored on the device
Combining many user requests into a single batched API call
Storing a recent response and reusing it instead of requesting again
quiz.explanation: Caching keeps a recent response and reuses it for a set time, which cuts cost, latency and rate-limit pressure. Batching also reduces the number of calls, but it combines requests rather than reusing earlier responses.

quiz.question: You are preparing for PM interviews. Why does technical fluency matter in many of them?
options: Interviewers often ask how a feature would work to test feasibility reasoning
Most PM interviews include a live coding round to check engineering skill
Interviewers mainly check that you can name specific languages and frameworks
It shows you can write the technical design so engineers don't need to
quiz.explanation: Many companies ask lighter system-design questions ('how would this feature work?') to see whether you can reason about feasibility and work well with engineers. Live coding rounds are uncommon for most PM roles, and naming technologies matters less than reasoning about how a feature works.

keyTakeaways: APIs = software's contracts; you can read them without coding
Know GET/POST, 4xx/5xx, JSON, caching, rate limits — 80% of PM technical talk
Always design the failure state for external dependencies

practicalTools.name: Rebuild & Critique
practicalTools.description: Learn design empathy by doing the work once
practicalTools.exercise: (1) In free Figma, recreate one screen of an app you use daily (Swiggy home, Spotify player...). Imperfect is fine — feel the decisions. (2) Then critique the original using the PM format: 'What works (2 things) / Questions (2) / Suggestions tied to user goals (2)'. Never say 'make it pop' — tie every point to a user task or metric.
practicalTools.deliverable: One Figma screen + a 6-point written critique

quiz.question: You are the PM for a checkout flow and are reviewing the designer's latest screens. Which piece of feedback is most useful?
options: Move the Pay button above the fold and make it larger so users notice it sooner.
60% of users drop off at this step. What options could reduce the friction?
Let's mirror the top competitor's checkout layout, since users already know it.
This step feels cluttered to me, so can we simplify the visuals before launch?
quiz.explanation: Strong PM feedback brings the problem and the evidence, then leaves the solution to the designer's expertise. Prescribing a specific fix like moving the button skips the designer's exploration and may not address why users actually drop off.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between a wireframe and a mockup?
options: A wireframe is a clickable flow; a mockup is a static image of one screen
A wireframe shows low-fi structure; a mockup shows high-fi visual design
A wireframe is the final handoff spec; a mockup is an early rough sketch
Both have the same fidelity, but a mockup swaps placeholder for real copy
quiz.explanation: Wireframes capture layout and structure cheaply, and mockups add the high-fidelity visual design. Clickability defines a prototype, not a wireframe, so the 'clickable flow' option confuses the two.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a clickable prototype?
options: Giving engineers the final pixel specs for development
Replacing the PRD as the source of feature requirements
Testing the flow with users before engineering builds it
Producing polished visuals for launch marketing assets
quiz.explanation: A prototype lets you watch real users go through a flow and fix problems while changes are still cheap, before any code is written. Final pixel specs come from the finished design handoff, not from a prototype built for testing.

quiz.question: A designer proposes a flow you personally dislike, but they back it with solid rationale. What should you do?
options: If stakes are high, test both with a few users; otherwise defer to them
Overrule it, since the PM is accountable for the final product decision
Escalate to your manager so a neutral party can break the deadlock
Mock up your preferred version in Figma and ask the team to vote on it
quiz.explanation: Disagreements about how users will behave are best settled by user evidence, and only when the stakes justify the effort. Otherwise you trust the designer's craft. Overruling on PM authority swaps your preference for their reasoned judgment and damages the partnership.

quiz.question: Each feature team at your company builds its own slightly different buttons and modals. Why should a PM support investing in a design system?
options: It lets PMs skip design review for most new features
It mainly helps engineering, so PM priorities are unaffected
Reusable components let teams ship consistent UI faster
It ensures every new feature is usable without testing
quiz.explanation: Shared components reduce design and build time for each feature and keep the product coherent. Consistent components do not make a flow usable on their own, so user testing is still needed.

quiz.question: In UI design, what does 'visual hierarchy' refer to?
options: Organizing Figma layers and frames into a clean nested structure
Using size, contrast, and position to set what users notice first
Ordering the screens in a flow from the entry point to the last step
Ranking design decisions by who on the team has final sign-off
quiz.explanation: Visual hierarchy guides the eye so users see the most important element first, such as the primary CTA. Nesting layers is file organization in Figma, not what users perceive on screen.

quiz.question: When should a designer ideally get involved in a new feature?
options: At problem discovery, so they help shape the solution space
Once the PRD is final, so they design to stable requirements
After engineering scopes it, so the designs stay buildable
Only for user-facing work; internal tools can skip design
quiz.explanation: Bringing design in during discovery means designers help solve the problem rather than decorate a fixed solution, which also prevents late rework. Waiting for a final PRD feels orderly but locks in a solution before design has explored the options.

quiz.question: What does auto-layout do in Figma?
options: Generates complete screen layouts automatically from a text prompt
Snaps objects to a fixed column grid as you drag them around a frame
Makes frames resize and space their children automatically, like real UI
Copies a frame's design across mobile and desktop sizes in one step
quiz.explanation: Auto-layout frames grow, shrink, and space their contents the way coded UI does, which makes designs easier to hand off to engineers. Snapping to a column grid is what layout grids do, which is a separate feature.

quiz.question: You are giving PM feedback in a design critique of a new onboarding screen. Which structure works best?
options: A prioritized list of every issue found, most severe ones first
Gut reactions from each attendee, followed by a vote on options
Your preferred visual changes, so the designer has clear direction
What works, open questions, and suggestions tied to user goals
quiz.explanation: A balanced critique that ties every point to a user goal or metric improves the design and keeps trust high. A list of only problems is thorough, but it skips what to keep and pushes the session toward fault-finding.

quiz.question: To hit a launch date, your team proposes pushing all accessibility work to a later release. What is the strongest PM response?
options: Agree, since accessibility is polish best added once usage is validated
Hand it to the legal team, since accessibility is mainly a compliance task
Agree, as long as the product does not serve government or public users
Keep contrast, touch targets, and screen-reader support in the launch scope
quiz.explanation: Accessibility basics are table stakes. They widen the set of people who can use the product and cost far less to build in upfront than to retrofit. Treating them as post-launch polish shuts some users out and adds rework later.

keyTakeaways: Bring problems and evidence to designers, not solutions
Low-fi first: structure is cheap to change, pixels are not
Doing one screen in Figma yourself builds permanent empathy

practicalTools.name: Pricing Teardown + Design
practicalTools.description: Reverse-engineer real pricing, then create your own
practicalTools.exercise: (1) Tear down 3 pricing pages (e.g. Notion, Zomato Gold, Canva): what's the value metric? what forces an upgrade? what's the anchor tier? (2) Design 3-tier pricing for your capstone product: name the tiers, pick the value metric, decide what's free and why. Write 3 sentences defending your value metric.
practicalTools.deliverable: 3 teardown notes + your own 3-tier pricing table with rationale

quiz.question: In pricing, a 'value metric' is best described as:
options: The unit you charge along that grows as the customer gets more value
Your cost to serve each user, used to set a minimum price floor
Total monthly recurring revenue, tracked to measure business growth
The engagement metric you report to show how widely the product is adopted
quiz.explanation: A value metric (seats, messages, GMV, events) is the axis you charge along. It rises as customers get more value, so expansion revenue comes naturally and the price feels fair. Cost to serve sets a price floor, but it says nothing about value received.

quiz.question: Value-based pricing means:
options: Adding a fixed margin on top of your cost to build and serve the product
Setting price from the value customers get, discovered through research
Pricing slightly below key competitors to win share in the market
Setting the price at whatever level maximizes sign-ups at launch
quiz.explanation: Value-based pricing starts from what the product is worth to the customer and tests willingness to pay through research. Cost-plus, the most tempting distractor, ignores willingness to pay, and competitor-based pricing hands your strategy to someone else.

quiz.question: You are deciding whether to launch a product as freemium. Freemium tends to work best when:
options: Paid acquisition is unaffordable, whatever free users cost to serve
The product is costly to serve, so free users can sample premium value
The core value only shows up after weeks of setup and guided onboarding
Serving free users is cheap and their usage builds habit or network effects
quiz.explanation: Freemium pays off when free users cost little to serve and either convert or bring in others through habit or network effects. Without that, it is just expensive charity. Choosing it only because you can't afford paid acquisition ignores serving costs and conversion, and products that need slow setup usually do better with a trial or sales-assisted motion.

quiz.question: On a three-tier pricing page, you add a 'Most popular' badge to the middle tier. What is it mainly doing?
options: Acting as a neutral label that does not change which tier buyers pick
Using social proof to nudge more buyers toward the middle tier
Signalling that the middle tier is temporarily discounted versus the others
Changing the packaging by altering which features the middle tier includes
quiz.explanation: The badge signals what other buyers chose, so it nudges people toward the highlighted 'safe' middle option and raises average deal size. Treating it as a neutral label misses that how a pricing page is presented shapes choice as much as the price does.

quiz.question: You are moving an API product to usage-based pricing. What is customers' most common concern, and the typical mitigation?
options: Paying for unused seats; mitigate by moving customers onto annual contracts
Too few features at entry level; mitigate by adding a premium feature tier
Unpredictable bills; mitigate with spend caps, usage alerts, and cost calculators
Slow onboarding; mitigate by offering a longer free trial before billing starts
quiz.explanation: With uncapped variable bills, customers worry about a surprise invoice. Good usage-based pricing therefore includes ways to keep costs predictable. Paying for unused seats is a seat-based pricing problem, and usage-based pricing is usually adopted to avoid it.

quiz.question: You raise prices 20% for all customers, and churn stays flat over the next quarter. What is the most reasonable inference?
options: You were probably underpriced, but watch renewals and new sign-ups before going further
Customers are clearly price-insensitive, so another increase next quarter is low-risk
The increase fully succeeded, because flat churn shows the revenue impact is settled
Flat churn tells you nothing about pricing, because churn is a lagging metric
quiz.explanation: Flat churn suggests customers valued the product more than you charged. But annual customers may not have renewed yet, and new-customer conversion may drop, so you should keep watching before raising again. Planning another increase right away reads too much into one quarter of data.

quiz.question: During a price change, 'grandfathering' existing customers means:
options: Moving all existing customers to the new price right away, after giving advance notice
Giving long-tenured customers a loyalty discount on top of the new, higher price
Letting existing customers keep their old price while new customers pay the new rate
Refunding existing customers once for the difference between the old and new price
quiz.explanation: Grandfathering keeps current customers on their existing price while new customers pay the new rate. It gives up some revenue in exchange for trust and retention. A loyalty discount on the new price is a different tactic, because those customers still move to the new price structure.

quiz.question: You are designing good / better / best tiers for a SaaS product. Which of these is a packaging decision rather than a pricing decision?
options: Setting the Pro tier at ₹499 versus ₹599 per user per month
Choosing between a 15% and a 20% discount for annual billing
Deciding which features go in the Pro tier versus the Enterprise tier
Showing prices in local currency for each market you launch in
quiz.explanation: Packaging decides what goes in each tier, and pricing decides what each tier costs. The annual-discount option is the most tempting distractor, but it changes the price paid, not what the customer gets.

quiz.question: You are pricing a B2B product analytics tool. Which value metric is the strongest candidate?
options: Dashboard views per month, since views show the tool is being actively used
Integrations connected, since more connections show a deeper product setup
Support tickets filed, since heavier customers need more help from your team
Tracked events, since event volume grows as the customer's own product grows
quiz.explanation: Tracked events grow with the customer's own scale, so the price follows the value they get. Charging for dashboard views sounds usage-based, but it penalises customers for using the tool more, which works against adoption.

quiz.question: In a PM interview you're asked, 'How would you price this new product?' Which opening best shows the business sense being tested?
options: Start by sizing the TAM to estimate how much total revenue is possible
Take the company's revenue target and divide it by expected customers to set a price
Start by choosing between a freemium model and a time-limited free trial
Clarify the target customers and the value they get, then pick a value metric
quiz.explanation: Strong answers begin with who the customer is and what value they get, because that decides both what to charge for and how much. Dividing a revenue target by expected customers is tempting, but it ignores willingness to pay. TAM sizing and the freemium-versus-trial choice come later, once value is clear.

keyTakeaways: Price along the axis where the customer gets value
Packaging and anchoring shape choice as much as the number does
Pricing is a product feature — research it, test it, iterate it

practicalTools.name: Spec an AI Feature End-to-End
practicalTools.description: The exercise that turns 'interested in AI' into a portfolio artifact
practicalTools.exercise: Pick a real product you use (e.g. a food-delivery app). Spec one AI feature: (1) user problem + why AI beats rules here (2) approach: which model API, what context/data goes in the prompt (3) draft the actual prompt (4) eval plan: 10 test cases with expected outputs, including 3 adversarial ones (5) guardrails: hallucination policy, fallback UX when confidence is low, and 2 quality metrics you'd track post-launch.
practicalTools.deliverable: A 2-page AI feature spec with prompt + 10-case eval table

quiz.question: When should a feature use AI instead of rules?
options: When inputs are fuzzy or open-ended and rules would explode in complexity
When the logic is well-defined but would take engineers a long time to code
When the output must be exactly reproducible and auditable every time
When competitors have shipped AI features and users now expect parity
quiz.explanation: AI is worth its cost and unpredictability when input is unstructured and varied, so rules can't keep up. Logic that is well-defined or must be reproducible is better served by rules, which are cheaper and testable. Matching competitors is not a reason on its own.

quiz.question: In an LLM-powered feature, a hallucination is:
options: The model confidently generating plausible but false information
The model refusing to answer a request it judges to be unsafe
The model giving different answers to the same prompt each time
The model repeating sensitive data it saw in its training set
quiz.explanation: LLMs generate plausible text, not verified truth, so they can state made-up facts with confidence. Different answers to the same prompt is non-determinism, not hallucination, because each of those answers may still be accurate.

quiz.question: An 'eval' for an AI feature is:
options: A one-time benchmark score published by the model provider
A post-launch survey asking users how satisfied they are with answers
A repeatable test suite that scores outputs against expected results
The confidence score the model attaches to each of its own outputs
quiz.explanation: Evals act as acceptance criteria for non-deterministic software: a repeatable set of cases you rerun whenever a prompt or model changes. A vendor's benchmark score is generic and one-off, so it can't tell you whether your feature works on your use cases.

quiz.question: Your AI meeting-notes summary feature gets about 8% of eval cases wrong. What is the best product response?
options: Hold the launch until engineering cuts the error rate to zero on the eval set
Ship with source links and easy correction, then track how errors affect users
Ship as is, since 92% accuracy beats most summaries people write by hand
Ship with an 'AI can make mistakes' disclaimer shown under every summary
quiz.explanation: Designing for fallibility means helping users spot and recover from errors, then measuring the real impact of those errors. A generic disclaimer is tempting, but it puts the whole burden on users without helping them catch mistakes. A zero error rate is not a realistic bar for LLM output.

quiz.question: In AI evals, 'LLM-as-judge' means:
options: Having the production model rate its own confidence before answering
Asking users to vote on which of two model answers they prefer
Having legal reviewers approve every prompt before it goes live
Using a model to grade other model outputs against a rubric at scale
quiz.explanation: LLM-as-judge is a scalable eval technique: a separate model scores outputs against a rubric, and humans spot-check the judge. A model rating its own confidence is self-assessment, not a rubric-based grade, and it is often poorly calibrated.

quiz.question: Which is a guardrail metric for the quality and safety of an AI assistant?
options: Weekly active users of the assistant feature
Average number of messages per conversation
Share of responses users flag as wrong or harmful
Number of new prompt versions deployed per sprint
quiz.explanation: Guardrail metrics watch for harm, such as wrong answers or unsafe content, while success metrics track value. Messages per conversation is ambiguous: a rise could mean engagement or users struggling to get a correct answer, so it doesn't directly measure quality or safety.

quiz.question: Why does the context you put into the prompt matter so much for an AI feature?
options: More context always improves answers, so include as much product data as you can
Context permanently updates the model, so later users benefit from what you add
Context mainly controls tone and format rather than the accuracy of the answers
The model knows only its training data plus what you supply, so relevant context cuts errors
quiz.explanation: Putting the right user and product data into the prompt often improves results more than switching models. More isn't always better, because irrelevant or excessive context can distract the model and raise cost. Prompt context also never retrains the model.

quiz.question: On an AI feature team, which split of ownership between the PM and ML engineers is most appropriate?
options: PM owns the problem, quality bar and user trust; engineers own models and infrastructure
PM owns the UX and launch timing; ML engineers own the models and set the quality bar
PM picks the model architecture and training approach; engineers implement and deploy it
PM and ML engineers co-own every decision equally, with no single owner of the quality bar
quiz.explanation: The PM defines what 'good' means based on user needs and decides how users experience uncertainty, and engineers build the system that meets that bar. Letting engineers set the quality bar is tempting, but it gives away the PM's core job of setting acceptance criteria from user needs.

quiz.question: A senior stakeholder says 'add AI to everything.' What is your best response?
options: Add AI to the highest-traffic screens first so the investment reaches the most users
Find where fuzzy-input problems exist, prototype the top one, and eval it before scaling
Launch a lightweight AI chatbot across the product to show momentum, then iterate
Push back until AI models mature enough to make every use case low-risk
quiz.explanation: Treat AI like any other capability: start from the problem, gate on evidence, and begin where AI clearly beats the alternatives. Starting with high-traffic screens is tempting, but traffic says nothing about whether AI solves a real problem there better than rules.

quiz.question: Your AI feature's output quality is mediocre. What is usually the cheapest way to improve it?
options: Fine-tune or train a custom model on your own product data
Move to a self-hosted open model on dedicated GPU infrastructure
Raise the model's temperature so answers become more varied
Improve the prompts, the context retrieval and the output constraints
quiz.explanation: Prompt and context engineering usually deliver the early wins at low cost. Fine-tuning is tempting, but it is slow and costly and usually comes after prompts and context have been exhausted. Raising temperature adds randomness, not quality.

keyTakeaways: AI is a capability, not a strategy — problem first
No evals, no launch: define 'good' before you build
Design for fallibility: confidence, sources, fallbacks, guardrail metrics

practicalTools.name: The 2-Week Real Project
practicalTools.description: Everything from Days 1-35 applied once, for real
practicalTools.exercise: Week 1 — DISCOVER: (1) Pick a real problem you or people around you have. (2) Run 5 Mom-Test interviews (Day 4). (3) Write problem statement + bottom-up sizing (Day 6). (4) Competitive scan of 3 alternatives (Day 12). Week 2 — BUILD & TEST: (5) Write a 1-page PRFAQ press release (Day 2) and mini-PRD with success metrics (Days 13/15). (6) Build a Figma prototype or no-code landing page (Day 33). (7) Show it to 3 target users; record reactions and one metric (e.g. 'would you use this weekly?'). (8) Write the case study. SELF-GRADE RUBRIC (out of 100): problem clarity 25, research evidence 25, solution reasoning 20, metrics thinking 15, storytelling 15. Below 70? Revise the weakest section once before publishing.
practicalTools.deliverable: Published case study (Notion/Google Doc) with interview quotes, prototype link, test results, and your rubric score

quiz.question: You are switching into PM. Why does one real capstone project usually help you more than finishing another PM course?
options: It adds a recognized credential that recruiters filter for when screening applications
It teaches more frameworks than a course, which broadens your theoretical PM knowledge
It gives evidence of your judgment with real users under uncertainty, which interviews probe
It lets you list formal product management job experience on your resume
quiz.explanation: Interviewers test how you handled ambiguity and real users, and a shipped cycle gives you true stories to tell. A project is not a credential and not formal job experience. Its value is evidence of judgment, not more theory.

quiz.question: In your capstone discovery, 3 of your 5 interviewees turn out not to have the problem you assumed. What should you do?
options: Discount the result, since five interviews is too small a sample to change direction
Narrow to the segment that does have it or reframe the problem, and document the pivot
Keep the original problem and recruit interviewees who seem more likely to have it
Continue building the solution and add a survey later to quantify the demand
quiz.explanation: An invalidated assumption is a finding. Narrowing the segment or reframing the problem, then documenting the pivot honestly, makes a stronger case study than smooth confirmation. Waving it away as a small sample means ignoring the only real evidence you have, when it should shape your next round of research.

quiz.question: You are choosing a problem for your 2-week capstone. Which choice is best?
options: A specific problem you see weekly and can reach five real users about
A large-market startup idea that would be attractive to early investors
A trending space like AI agents, where recruiters expect to see projects
A novel problem that no existing product has attempted to solve yet
quiz.explanation: The capstone is about producing evidence, so a problem you can quickly reach real users for beats a glamorous idea. A large-market or trending idea feels impressive, but if you can't get interviews and tests done in two weeks, there's no case study.

quiz.question: For your capstone's user test, what should your prototype be?
options: A polished high-fidelity design, so users judge it like a real product
A working coded MVP, so you can measure real usage over several weeks
A complete clickable prototype covering every screen and edge case
The cheapest artifact that gets honest reactions to the core flow
quiz.explanation: You are testing the value hypothesis, not engineering or design skill, so build the cheapest thing that shows the core flow. A polished or coded version costs time that should go to talking with users, and it adds little to what a two-week test can learn.

quiz.question: You show your prototype to 3 target users. Which data from the sessions is most valuable?
options: Their ratings of how likely they are to use the product regularly in future
Their suggestions for which features you should add to the product next
Their overall impressions of the design, layout and visual polish
Where they hesitate or misunderstand, plus specifics of how they handle it today
quiz.explanation: Observed behavior and concrete past actions are reliable, and the Mom Test applies to prototypes as much as to interviews. Likelihood-to-use ratings are hypothetical opinions, and users tend to overstate them to be polite.

quiz.question: How should your capstone case study be structured, given that recruiters skim it?
options: Lead with the problem and who has it, then research, decisions and outcome
Lead with the final prototype screens, then the process that produced them
Lead with your background and why you want to move into product management
Lead with the tools and methods you used, then the findings they produced
quiz.explanation: Opening with the problem shows you think from the user back, and it follows the problem, research, decisions, outcome arc that recruiters look for. Opening with prototype screens is solution-first, and it hides the reasoning that the case study exists to show.

quiz.question: You self-grade your capstone case study at 62/100. Your rubric says to revise anything below 70, and one section scores far lower than the others. What is the best next move?
options: Publish now, since shipping matters more than a self-assigned score
Revise the weakest-scoring section once, then publish the case study
Rework every section until the total clears 90, then publish it
Start over on a different problem that should produce clearer evidence
quiz.explanation: One focused pass on the clearly weakest section closes the biggest gap for the least effort, and then you ship. Publishing as is knowingly ships a weak spot, while reworking everything to 90 delays publishing for small gains.

quiz.question: You put up a no-code landing page to test demand for your capstone idea. Which success metric should you track?
options: Total unique visitors you drove to the page during the test window
Commitment signals like email signups or pre-orders from target users
Average time on page, as a measure of how engaged visitors were
Positive comments and likes when you share the page on social media
quiz.explanation: A commitment signal from target users tells real demand apart from polite interest. Traffic and time on page mostly reflect how you promoted the page, not whether anyone wants the product.

quiz.question: How should your capstone project appear on your resume?
options: As a full-time 'Product Manager' role at a startup named after your project
As a line in your skills section listing the frameworks the project used
As a project entry with concrete, honest results from your interviews and tests
Left off the resume and mentioned only if an interviewer asks about projects
quiz.explanation: A clearly labeled project with concrete results, such as how many people you interviewed and what testers actually did, gives interviewers something real to ask about. Presenting it as a full-time job is a misrepresentation that falls apart under questioning, and leaving it off wastes your strongest evidence.

quiz.question: Which capstone mistake is hardest to recover from?
options: Skipping real users and validating the idea with your own opinions
Choosing a problem too small to seem interesting to recruiters
Building the prototype in a no-code tool rather than real code
Running past the two-week timebox before writing the case study
quiz.explanation: Without real user contact there's no evidence, so the whole case study is fiction. A small problem or a slipped timeline can still be framed well and fixed, but missing user evidence can't be faked after the fact.

keyTakeaways: One shipped cycle with real users outweighs 29 days of study
Invalidated assumptions, documented honestly, impress interviewers most
The case study is the deliverable — write for a skimming recruiter

practicalTools.name: The 10-Rep Program
practicalTools.description: A structured drill schedule with self-grading
practicalTools.exercise: STEP 1 — Story bank: write 8 STAR stories from your work (a conflict, a data insight that changed a decision, a failure, an influence-without-authority moment...). STEP 2 — 10 recorded reps: 2 product design (use CIRCLES, Day 25), 2 execution/metric-drop (Day 30 video), 2 strategy, 2 behavioral, 2 estimation (Day 6). Record yourself, 6-8 min each. SELF-GRADE each rep out of 10: structure 3, user-centricity 3, communication 2, insight 2. Redo any rep under 6. STEP 3 — Humans: schedule at least 3 live mocks (Pramp/Exponent peer practice, or PM friends). One mock with a stranger is worth five alone.
practicalTools.deliverable: 8-story STAR bank + 10 graded recordings + 3 booked live mocks

quiz.question: Frameworks like CIRCLES exist mainly to:
options: Give you a script to recite step by step to the interviewer
Show the interviewer you know standard PM vocabulary
Guarantee a complete answer even without prior practice
Structure your thinking so no important step gets skipped
quiz.explanation: Frameworks are a scaffold that keeps your thinking complete. Use the structure quietly and keep the conversation natural. Reciting the framework step by step, the most tempting mistake, sounds scripted, and interviewers mark that down.

quiz.question: An interviewer asks you to 'Design a product for X.' What is the best first move?
options: List the core features you would build first
Estimate the market size to justify the product
Clarify the scope and identify the target user
Benchmark the main competitors' existing products
quiz.explanation: A strong design answer moves from scope and user to their problems and then to solutions. Jumping straight to features skips the user and their problem, which signals junior thinking.

quiz.question: In an execution interview you are told: 'Your key metric dropped 10% overnight.' What should your first branch be?
options: Brainstorm product fixes to recover the lost usage
Launch an A/B test to find which change caused it
Clarify the metric, then split internal vs external causes
Survey affected users to ask why they disengaged
quiz.explanation: Structured isolation comes before solutions. First confirm what the metric measures, then separate internal causes (a bug or release) from external ones (seasonality or a competitor). An A/B test is a tool for checking a hypothesis, not a first diagnostic step.

quiz.question: A strong STAR story spends most of its time on:
options: The specific actions you took and the measurable result
The situation, so the interviewer grasps the full context
The task, explaining the team's goals and constraints
The team's collective effort and each person's role
quiz.explanation: Interviewers are judging your decisions and their impact, so the Action and Result should get most of the time. Spending long on the Situation is a common trap. It uses up time without showing what you did.

quiz.question: In estimation questions, interviewers mainly grade:
options: Landing close to the true real-world number
Recalling accurate market statistics from memory
The logic of your assumptions and breakdown
Reaching a precise final number in one pass
quiz.explanation: In estimation, the reasoning is what gets graded: clear assumptions, a logical breakdown and a sanity check. Landing close to the real number is nice, but a well-reasoned estimate that misses still scores well.

quiz.question: An interviewer asks why someone from a data analyst background should be a PM. What is the strongest way to position your experience?
options: Show how your analysis shaped real product decisions
Admit the gap and stress how fast you're learning PM skills
Highlight the SQL and dashboarding skills you've mastered
Suggest starting as a product analyst to bridge the gap
quiz.explanation: Analyst-to-PM is a well-established path. Your strongest pitch is data-driven judgment that changed product decisions. Leading with tool skills like SQL makes you sound like an analyst, not a decision-maker.

quiz.question: Why is recording your solo practice answers valuable?
options: It lets you memorize a polished answer to replay later
It builds a portfolio you can share with recruiters
It gives enough feedback that live mocks become optional
You catch rambling and gaps you miss while speaking
quiz.explanation: Watching yourself back and grading against a rubric shows filler, rambling and missing structure that you can't notice while speaking. It adds to live mocks but does not replace them, because only live mocks add real-time pressure from another person.

quiz.question: You completely blank in the middle of an answer. What is the best recovery?
options: Apologize and ask to move on to a different question
Pause, recap what you've covered, and continue
Restart the whole answer from the beginning
Keep talking through it to avoid an awkward silence
quiz.explanation: A calm pause and recap ('So far we've covered X; next is Y') shows composure, and interviewers are assessing that too. Talking through it to fill the silence usually turns into rambling and weakens the structure further.

quiz.question: You've finished 10 recorded solo reps, all self-graded 7/10 or higher. What is the best next step before real interviews?
options: Do 10 more solo reps to push every score above 9
Do several live mocks with unfamiliar interviewers
Go straight to real interviews since scores are strong
Memorize your story bank word-for-word as scripts
quiz.explanation: Solo reps can't recreate a stranger's follow-up questions and real-time pressure, and live mocks expose those gaps. Adding more solo reps mostly polishes answers you already know well, and self-grades can overrate how ready you are.

quiz.question: What is the highest-value prep the night before a PM interview?
options: Learn a few new frameworks for unexpected questions
Review your story bank and their product, then rest
Do a full timed mock covering every question type
Memorize scripted answers to the likeliest questions
quiz.explanation: Fresh recall of your own stories and the company's product, plus good sleep, does more for performance than new material. Learning new frameworks or running a full mock at the last minute adds fatigue and confusion rather than confidence.

keyTakeaways: Stories and reps, not frameworks, pass interviews
Record → rubric → redo: the solo feedback loop
3+ live mocks with strangers before the real thing
